summary.text: The Industrial Revolution was the shift from hand production to machines and factories, beginning in Great Britain around 1760.
It brought more water and steam power, new iron and chemical processes and machine tools, and output rose greatly.
Textiles led the way, and by about 1840 the changes had spread to continental Europe and the United States.

facts.value: Textiles, the first to use modern production methods

items.prompt: Two historians give different start and end dates for the Industrial Revolution. What does that show?

options.label: One of them has confused it with the Second Industrial Revolution
The start was officially recorded, so one date must be wrong
The precise start and end really are debated among historians
The change began in separate years in every British town

items.explain: The precise start and end of the Industrial Revolution is debated among historians, as is the pace of the changes.

items.prompt: In the 1750s iron makers wanted more air blown into their furnaces than water wheels could supply. What did they turn to?

options.label: Engines that burned fuel to power the blast air
Larger water wheels set on faster rivers
Hand-worked bellows run by extra labourers
Rolling mills in place of hammering the iron

items.explain: The steam engine began powering blast air in the 1750s, which overcame the limit of water power and allowed a large increase in iron production.

items.prompt: An ironmaster stops burning charcoal in his furnace and uses coke instead. What does he gain?

options.label: Cheaper fuel, but he must keep his furnaces small
Stronger iron, but at a much higher fuel cost
Cast iron blowing cylinders he no longer needs
Lower fuel costs and room to build larger furnaces

items.explain: Coke in place of charcoal greatly lowered the fuel cost of making iron, and it allowed larger blast furnaces with economies of scale.

items.prompt: In the late 1830s growth slowed even though locomotives and steamships were spreading. What was behind the slowdown?

options.label: Steam power proved unreliable, so factories returned to hand production
Mechanised spinning and weaving had been widely adopted and markets matured
The new telegraph spread quickly and made further machines unnecessary
Britain lost its textile lead to rival manufacturers in Mughal India

items.explain: Adoption of early innovations such as mechanised spinning and weaving slowed as markets matured, and the telegraph was not enough to drive high growth.

items.prompt: Friedrich Engels wrote of an industrial revolution in 1844, yet the phrase stayed rare in everyday English for decades. Why?

options.label: His book was not translated into English until the late 19th century
His book was banned in Britain until Toynbee's lectures in 1881
British workers rejected a phrase that seemed to praise factory owners
A French envoy had used it first and kept it out of English speech

items.explain: Engels's book was not translated into English until the late 19th century, and the expression did not enter everyday language until then.

items.prompt: A factory adds an assembly line, mass production and electrical grid power. Which wave of change do these belong to?

options.label: The Second Agricultural Revolution that came before industry
The first wave, when hand production first gave way to machines
Proto-industrialisation in parts of Europe, Mughal India and China
The Second Industrial Revolution, which restarted rapid growth

items.explain: Rapid growth returned after 1870 from innovations of the Second Industrial Revolution, including steel-making, mass production, assembly lines and electrical grids.

paragraphs.heading: What it was
paragraphs.text: The Industrial Revolution was a period when the world economy moved toward manufacturing that was more widespread, efficient and stable. It followed the Second Agricultural Revolution and is sometimes called the First Industrial Revolution, to set it apart from the second one that came after it. It began in Great Britain around 1760 and had reached continental Europe and the United States by about 1840. At its heart was a move from making things by hand to making them with machines, along with new methods for chemicals and iron, more use of water and steam power, machine tools, and the mechanised factory.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: Economic historians agree that its start is the most important event in human history for material progress, rivalled only by the adoption of farming. Output soared, and population grew as never before. It reached into almost every part of life: average income and population began a long, steady rise, and living standards improved for most people in the Western world, though some argue real gains only came in the 20th century. It also shifted where things were made, from China and India before it to North America and Western Europe after it.

paragraphs.heading: Britain and cloth
paragraphs.text: Britain led the way. By the middle of the 1700s it was the leading commercial nation, with output per person, or GDP per capita, well above the world average, and many of the new inventions were British. Textiles were the first industry to use modern production methods and became the biggest by jobs, value of output and money invested. Britain took up machine spinning quickly in the 1780s, and the method spread to continental Europe and the US early in the next century. After 1800 steam power and iron production grew fast.

paragraphs.heading: How much faster
paragraphs.text: The gains were huge. Machine spinning of cotton, driven first by water and later by steam, raised output per worker about 500 times, the power loom raised it 40 times, and the cotton gin made pulling seeds out of cotton 50 times more productive. Steam engines grew efficient enough to burn only a fifth to a tenth as much fuel. Once stationary engines could drive rotary motion they suited factories, and the high-pressure engine, strong for its weight, suited transport.

paragraphs.heading: Iron and machine tools
paragraphs.text: Making iron changed too. Using coke in place of charcoal cut the fuel cost of making iron and allowed bigger blast furnaces, with the savings that come from working at scale. Puddling made structural iron more cheaply than the older finery forge, the rolling mill worked fifteen times faster than hammering, and hot blast, developed in 1828, greatly raised fuel efficiency. Meanwhile the first machine tools appeared: the screw-cutting lathe, the milling machine and the cylinder boring machine. They made precision metal parts affordable to produce, although interchangeable parts took decades more to master.

paragraphs.heading: Naming it
paragraphs.text: The name has its own story. Its earliest recorded use was in 1799, when the French envoy Louis-Guillaume Otto announced that France had joined the race to industrialise. Friedrich Engels used the phrase in 1844, and Arnold Toynbee's lectures of 1881 are credited with making it popular. Historians still argue about when it began and ended and how fast things changed, and some, such as John Clapham and Nicholas Crafts, say the change was gradual and that revolution is the wrong word.
